relevance_note: Table 2 gives individual clinical history for the study's HA20 patients ('Sixteen patients from 6 families of European ancestry with HA20 were studied'), though no per-patient variant is printed.
method_note: Individuals are the 16 HA20 patients of Table 2 ('Detailed clinical history of all 16 patients included'); labels are the verbatim values of its 'Patient number' column (1-16) and family labels the 'Family' column (1-6). A short Python script transcribed Table 2 rows into spans (row segment from the patient number through the cell) and I checked every row's values against the table by eye. Table 2 has no legend defining its 1/0 coding: cells '1' were read as present (the counts of 1s match the text: mouth ulcers 16, genital ulcers 13, gut symptoms 13, colchicine 5, adalimumab 5 = 'TNF-alpha blockers 5', six on immunosuppressants), while cells '0' were left 'not reported' under the v3 table-symbol rule, so no feature or treatment is marked absent. No TNFAIP3 variant, transcript or variant class is printed for any patient (the paper only says mutational status was extracted from medical records), so no variants rows were emitted; people are in scope by their HA20 diagnosis. Group-level findings (liver MRI in 5 patients, liver/stomach/ileal/colon histology, interferon signature in 5 patients, elevated liver enzymes in 4, 'no patient displayed auto-antibodies specific to PSC', one TNF-alpha-treated patient with sustained GI inflammation) cannot be attributed to numbered patients and were not recorded per person. Sex, ages and per-patient diagnosis basis are given only at group level (Table 1). Possible inconsistencies in the paper: Table 1 'Females 12 (71)' (12/16 is 75%) and controls 'Females 25 (78)' with n = 22; Table 1 'Abdominal pain 4 (25)' on collection day vs three patients with 'GI symptoms on collection day' = 1 in Table 2; text 'Elevated liver enzymes were noted in 4 patients' vs five patients with 'Liver disease' = 1 in Table 2 (possibly different measures); spleen lengths printed as '163 and 160 cm'. The paper does not say which of references 11-13 describes which family.
